resources.string: Paneth cells and the crypt barrier
Normal adult small intestine. This is an educational schematic: geometry, particles, and playback timing are illustrative, not measured or personal.
A Paneth cell sits low in the crypt wall. Its apical side faces the crypt lumen.
Secretory granules store antimicrobial substances near the apical surface, opposite the basal nucleus.
Granules fuse with the apical membrane and release their contents into the crypt lumen.
Released substances, including antimicrobial peptides, spread through the nearby crypt lumen and help protect the epithelial surface.
Paneth cell antimicrobial peptides in human tissue
Enteroendocrine cells: from lumen to blood
Normal adult small intestine; an open-type cell is shown. This educational diagram uses illustrative shapes, signals, and timing, not measured or personal data.
The narrow apical tip of this open-type cell contacts the crypt lumen and senses a chemical cue, such as a nutrient.
The luminal cue activates the cell. Hormone-containing vesicles are stored near the broader side facing the underlying tissue.
The hormone is released from the basal side into the nearby tissue. The luminal cue itself does not travel through the cell to the blood.
The released hormone can enter a nearby capillary and travel with blood to responsive cells elsewhere.

Intestinal stem cells renew the lining
Normal adult small intestine. This educational schematic uses illustrative cell counts, distances, and timing; it is not scaled to tissue or based on personal measurements.
A niche at the crypt base
Intestinal stem cells sit among neighboring cells, including Paneth cells, at the crypt base.
Stem-cell divisions maintain the base population and supply new descendants. This view follows one example of renewal.
Many descendants move toward a villus within the epithelial sheet. The stem-cell population stays near the base.
Some descendants mature into absorptive cells with a brush border, replacing older cells in the villus lining.
